cases.input: My iPhone is connected to Wi-Fi but says No Internet Connection.

guidance.summary: This describes a connection setting or problem, not evidence of a scam.
cautions: Joining Wi-Fi does not guarantee internet access or a trustworthy network.

next_actions.text: Open Settings > Wi-Fi and check whether Wi-Fi is on. Check the displayed network name; this does not confirm internet access.

evidence.title: iPhone Wi-Fi connection troubleshooting
evidence.quote: If an iPhone cannot connect to Wi-Fi, open Settings, Wi-Fi and check that Wi-Fi is on. A blue checkmark beside a network name indicates that the phone joined that network; it does not by itself prove that internet access works.

next_actions.text: If this is a network you recognize, check whether another device on the same network can access the internet.

evidence.title: iPhone Wi-Fi connection troubleshooting
evidence.quote: For a No Internet Connection message, try the same network on another device to see whether the problem is limited to the iPhone.

retrieved.title: Join a known Wi-Fi network on iPhone
retrieved.excerpt: To join a Wi-Fi network on iPhone, open Settings, Wi-Fi and turn Wi-Fi on. Choose a network that you recognize, then enter its password if prompted. Some public networks also ask you to accept terms before connection.

retrieved.title: Safari pop-up guidance for iPhone
retrieved.excerpt: Safari pop-ups on iPhone can be ordinary ads or deceptive warnings. A warning, prize, or technical-support phone number displayed by a webpage is not proof that the phone is infected. If a pop-up is unfamiliar, avoid its links and buttons; even a close button may be fake. Close the Safari tab or window instead. To review Safari protection settings, open Settings, Apps, Safari, then check Block Pop-ups and Fraudulent Website Warning.

retrieved.title: FTC: How To Spot, Avoid, and Report Tech Support Scams
retrieved.excerpt:
Real security pop-up warnings and messages will never ask you to call a phone number.

Not sure if it’s a scam? Talk to someone you trust — a friend, a family member, a neighbor. Talking about it could help you realize it's a scam.

If you think there may be a problem with your computer, update your computer’s security software and run a scan.

analysis.explanation:
In the past, if you used a public Wi-Fi network to get online, your information was at risk. That’s because most websites didn’t use encryption to scramble the data and protect it from hackers snooping on the network.

Today, most websites do use encryption to protect your information. Because of the widespread use of encryption, connecting through a public Wi-Fi network is usually safe.

retrieved.title: FTC: How To Secure Your Home Wi-Fi Network
retrieved.excerpt:
Turn on your router firewall. A firewall is an additional layer of protection that can help keep out viruses, malware, and even hackers. Most routers come with built-in firewalls, so check your settings to make sure your router’s firewall is turned on.

Protect your devices. Just as hackers can get to your data through unsecured networks, they can also get to your network through unsecured devices.

retrieved.title: FTC: How To Avoid a Scam
retrieved.excerpt:
Resist the pressure to act immediately. Honest businesses will give you time to make a decision. Anyone who pressures you to pay or give them your personal information is a scammer.

Know how scammers tell you to pay. Never pay someone who insists that you can only pay with cryptocurrency , a wire transfer service like Western Union or MoneyGram, a payment app , or a gift card .

retrieved.title: FTC: How to Recognize and Report Spam Text Messages
retrieved.excerpt:
Scammers might

promise free prizes , gift cards , or coupons — but they’re not real

offer you a low or no interest credit card — but there’s no deal and probably no card

promise to help you pay off your student loans — but they won’t

Scammers also send fake messages that say they have information about your account or a transaction.
